summary: Psalm 116 is a personal thanksgiving from someone who was near death, cried to Yahweh, and was rescued. The speaker moves from love and distress to rest, public vows, and praise in Jerusalem. The chapter ends with thanksgiving brought into the worshiping community rather than kept as a private feeling.
whyItMatters: This psalm shows how Book V of Psalms gives rescued worshipers words for answering God publicly. It joins danger, prayer, gratitude, and temple praise without explaining every detail of the crisis.

context.author: Anonymous within the psalm itself; Psalms as a book is an anthology with many writers and collections.
context.audience: Israel's worshiping and instructed community, later adopted by Jewish and Christian communities for public prayer and private life.
context.date: The Psalter contains poems from multiple periods and was shaped over time; this chapter should not be assigned one certain date from this chapter alone.
context.setting: A speaker remembers mortal danger and speaks vows in the presence of the people, in the courts of Yahweh's house in Jerusalem.
context.literaryForm: Hebrew poetic thanksgiving within the Psalms, using first-person testimony, repeated vows, and public praise.

outline.heading: Love Because Yahweh Listened
outline.note: The speaker begins with love for Yahweh because Yahweh heard his voice and cries, so he resolves to keep calling on him.

outline.heading: Death, Distress, and a Cry for Rescue
outline.note: The speaker describes being surrounded by death and Sheol, then recalls the plea: “Yahweh, I beg you, deliver my soul.”

outline.heading: Rescue Remembered and Rest Restored
outline.note: The psalm names Yahweh as gracious, righteous, and merciful, then tells the soul to return to rest because life, tears, and footing have been preserved.

outline.heading: Affliction and Human Unreliability
outline.note: The speaker looks back on severe affliction and a hasty conclusion that all people are liars.

outline.heading: Public Response to Yahweh's Benefits
outline.note: The question of repayment leads to the cup of salvation, calling on Yahweh's name, and paying vows before the people.

outline.heading: Servant Freed for Thanksgiving
outline.note: The speaker reflects on the death of Yahweh's saints, identifies as Yahweh's servant, and promises a sacrifice of thanksgiving.

outline.heading: Vows in Jerusalem
outline.note: The psalm closes by repeating the vow to pay vows publicly, locating that praise in Yahweh's house and in Jerusalem.

keyVerses.text: I love Yahweh, because he listens to my voice, and my cries for mercy.
keyVerses.why: This opening gives the reason for the whole psalm: love grows from being heard in distress.

keyVerses.text: For you have delivered my soul from death, my eyes from tears, and my feet from falling.
keyVerses.why: This verse gathers the rescue into three concrete images: life spared, grief answered, and stability restored.

keyVerses.text: What will I give to Yahweh for all his benefits toward me?
keyVerses.why: This question turns the psalm from remembering rescue toward public gratitude and fulfilled vows.

keyVerses.text: in the courts of Yahweh’s house, in the middle of you, Jerusalem. Praise Yah!
keyVerses.why: The ending places the speaker's thanksgiving in public worship at Jerusalem.

questions.question: Who is speaking in this psalm?
questions.answer: The chapter presents a first-person speaker who says he was brought low, cried to Yahweh, and was saved. The psalm itself does not name the speaker. In Psalms, the “I” can be an individual worshiper, a representative voice, or a prayer later taken up by the community.

questions.question: What danger had the speaker faced?
questions.answer: The psalm describes the danger with images of death, Sheol, trouble, sorrow, tears, falling, chains, and being brought low. It does not specify whether the crisis was illness, violence, imprisonment, or another mortal threat. The point the chapter states clearly is that the speaker experienced it as a life-threatening distress and believed Yahweh delivered him.

questions.question: What does “Sheol” mean here?
questions.answer: In this verse, Sheol belongs to the psalm's death imagery: “The cords of death” and “the pains of Sheol” surround the speaker. The chapter does not give a detailed map of the afterlife. A first reading should hear it as the realm or grip of death pressing in on the speaker.

questions.question: Why does the speaker say, “Return to your rest, my soul”?
questions.answer: The speaker addresses his own soul after recalling that Yahweh saved him. “Rest” here is the settled state that follows rescue, not an escape from the world. The next verse explains the reason: Yahweh has delivered the speaker from death, tears, and falling.

questions.question: Does “All people are liars” mean the psalm teaches that every human statement is false?
questions.answer: The verse says the speaker said this “in my haste,” during a moment of pressure. Readers differ on how strongly to take the line: some hear a broad statement about human unreliability, while others stress that it is the speech of panic rather than a calm doctrine. The chapter itself frames it as something said amid affliction.

questions.question: What is the “cup of salvation”?
questions.answer: The psalm does not explain a ritual in detail, but the phrase appears as part of the speaker's public response to Yahweh's benefits. It is paired with calling on Yahweh's name and paying vows before the people. Readers should avoid importing later uses of cup imagery as if they were already settled here.

questions.question: What are the vows the speaker will pay?
questions.answer: The chapter does not list the content of the vows. It tells us where and how they will be fulfilled: “in the presence of all his people,” and finally in the courts of Yahweh's house in Jerusalem. The repeated line shows that private rescue leads to public thanksgiving.

questions.question: What does “Precious in Yahweh’s sight is the death of his saints” mean?
questions.answer: The line comes after a testimony that Yahweh rescued the speaker from death, so it should not be read as if God is indifferent to the death of faithful people. “Precious” here marks the death of Yahweh's saints as weighty or important in Yahweh's sight. Readers differ over whether the verse emphasizes God's care that prevents such death, God's valuation of his people even in death, or both.

questions.question: Why does the psalm end in Jerusalem?
questions.answer: The speaker's thanksgiving is not only internal; it is brought into the public worship space. Verse 19 names “the courts of Yahweh’s house” and “Jerusalem,” placing the vow-payment and praise among the people. This fits the Psalms' wider use as voiced prayer for individuals and assemblies.

glossary.def: The divine name used throughout this translation of the psalm; the speaker loves, calls on, thanks, and vows to Yahweh.
The speaker's urgent pleas in distress, heard by Yahweh according to the opening verse.
A term used in verse 3 within the psalm's death imagery, where the speaker feels seized by the powers of death.
The speaker's life or self in the poem, the one needing deliverance and later told to return to rest.
Promises the speaker intends to fulfill publicly before Yahweh and the people.
The offering named in verse 17 as part of the speaker's response to being rescued.
